item.title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Response coefficients derived strictly from an unbiased reference circuit predict finite-bias circuit-level logical error rates with a median fold error of 1.09, cutting physical qubit counts by up to 42.4% (standard depolarizing) and 26.2% (superconducting-inspired) relative to square codes at physical error rate p=0.004 and target logical error rate PL,target=10−3.

Grade 0.520 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Youshin Chung, Yujin Kang, Jun Heo

Figure

Physical qubit count as a function of idle noise bias for validated rectangular surface codes versus unrotated square code baselines at p=0.004 and PL,target=10−3.

Asks

Can the logical error response to a localized circuit-level bias be inferred from an unbiased reference circuit and transferred to finite-bias conditions without geometry- or bias-specific response fitting?

Before

Neglecting bias response gives a median fold error of 1.28, while mapping the full idle-channel change directly into the baseline parameter yields 3.18.

But

Unrotated rectangular surface codes only; evaluated at bias ratios η∈{1,2,3}, 0.003≤p≤0.008, and for memory experiments run over r=max⁡(L1,L2) rounds.

Tools

Stim and PyMatching · Score-function logical sensitivity estimation · Ordinary least-squares regression · Sinter Monte Carlo sampling

Abstract

Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

item.title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Certifies exact code distances up to d=34 for stabilizer codes up to n=5278 physical qubits, verifying 88 of 95 surveyed lifted-product codes previously known only by distance upper bounds, within seconds per code on one Apple M3 Pro core.

Grade 0.506 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jong Yeon Lee

Figure

Search time scaled to an Apple M3 Pro reference core against exclusion cutoff weight W (left) and fraction of overlapping parity-check pairs (right) across multiple quantum LDPC code families.

Asks

Can minimum distances of large quantum low-density parity-check stabilizer codes be practically certified by exact branch-and-bound tree searches rather than bounded by heuristic witnesses?

Before

Randomized searches and linked-cluster tree searches (Dumer, Kovalev, Pryadko) provided upper bounds or scaled poorly for d≳16; exact values for many lifted-product codes remained uncertified.

But

CSS codes and non-CSS qubit stabilizer codes with sparse parity-check matrices; searches become prohibitive when check-pair overlap is low or distance exceeds accessible branch-depth budgets.

Tools

weighted-check lower bounds · stabilizer-equivalence pruning · verified permutation symmetry reduction · depth-first branch-and-bound search

Abstract

We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff W, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most W or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the [[144,12,12]] code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

item.title: Magic state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape on superconducting hardware
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Lattice-surgery escape into a distance-5 rotated surface code achieves a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% at roughly 11% average shot retainment, maintaining T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds post-escape at about 5% retainment.

Grade 0.505 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Haoran Liao, Michael Schutzman, William Munizzi, Pranav Mundada, Gavin Hartnett, Yuval Baum

Figure

Logical error rate per stabilizer round pL plotted against shot retainment under increasing complementary-gap postselection thresholds (left), and peak T-state fidelity plotted across rounds N (right). Lattice-surgery escape maintains higher fidelity and lower error rate at matched retainment than grafting variants.

Asks

Can magic state cultivation use lattice surgery to escape directly into a surface code on superconducting hardware, and how does it compare experimentally to grafting?

Before

Cultivated Steane-code T-state logical error probability was nearly 10x higher with roughly 3x lower retainment, and distance-5 grafting had 2x higher error rate per round (Rosenfeld 2024).

But

Requires complementary-gap postselection filtering out low-confidence decoder shots, reducing retainment down to 5–11%; execution limited to N≤10 stabilizer rounds.

Tools

IBM Nighthawk superconducting processor · lattice surgery escape · minimum-weight perfect matching · complementary-gap postselection (CGP) · superdense stabilizer extraction

Abstract

Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

item.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Keeping alternative physical gate realizations uncommitted until physical routing reaches an executable layout reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8% and physical circuit depth by 8.8--10.1% across 25 dual-rail workloads.

Grade 0.504 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Evan McKinney, Kun Liu, Harshvardhan K. Babla, Robert J. Schoelkopf, Yongshan Ding

Figure

Bar charts showing relative percentage reductions in routing SWAPs (panels a-c) and physical circuit depth (panels e-g) achieved by PRISM over Greedy across 25 benchmarks on grid, hexagonal, and heavy-hex architectures.

Asks

How can quantum compilers resolve the phase-ordering conflict between logical gate expansion into physical circuits and physical routing?

Before

Greedy search that fixes physical gate realizations before routing.

But

Realizations must act on fixed wires without internal SWAPs; unresolved gates sharing a logical qubit remain in program order; SABRE heuristic does not guarantee an optimal route.

Tools

boundary intermediate representation · dual-rail cavity qubits · SABRE physical routing heuristic · simple quotient graph availability mapping

Code. https://github.com/Yale-QCS/prism

Abstract

Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical CR_z has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

item.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Demonstrated fault-tolerant lattice-surgery teleportation between two distance-three surface-code logical qubits on a 41-transmon chip. Circuit depletion improved logical success probabilities from 0.57 to 0.65 for Z basis states and from 0.66 to 0.73 for X basis states.

Grade 0.488 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert, Jonathan Trebst, Franccois Swiadek, Felix Henrich, Dante Colao Zanúz, Mohsen Bahrami Panah, Lukas Bödeker, Nicholas Gialouris, Chrysander D. Hagen, Marek Pechal, Jean Claude Besse, Markus Müller, Christoph Hellings, Andreas Wallraff

Figure

Error-corrected logical expectation values across three teleportation circuits (fully modular, partially depleted, and fully depleted) for four logical eigenstates. Depleting non-essential stabilizer rounds increases teleported output fidelity.

Asks

How do logical observables evolve throughout fault-tolerant lattice surgery, and can circuit depletion optimize logical teleportation performance?

Before

Fully modular logical teleportation circuit achieved logical expectation values of |obreak⟨mSmZZˆL2⟩|=0.14 and |⟨mXXˆL2⟩|=0.32.

But

Demonstrated for Pauli eigenstates only; full quantum state tomography not implemented. Physical error rates remain above fault-tolerance threshold.

Tools

41 frequency-tunable transmon superconducting circuit · distance-three rotated planar surface code · flux-activated CZ gates · multiplexed dispersive readout with Purcell filters · lattice surgery

Abstract

Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Decoder switching using cluster-norm confidence cuts logical error rates by up to 3 to 4 orders of magnitude over BP-LSD and 2 to 3 orders over Beamsearch at physical error rate p=2×10−3 on bivariate bicycle codes.

Grade 0.464 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Arianna Meinking, Evangelia Takou, Kenneth R. Brown

Figure

Ratio of the per-cycle logical error rate of BP-LSD to that of the decoder-switching protocol plotted against switch rate for five bivariate bicycle codes at physical error rate p=2×10−3. Higher values indicate stronger error suppression from switching to Relay-BP or Tesseract.

Asks

Can available classical decoding time budgets in trapped-ion architectures be exploited via decoder switching to maximize logical error suppression on quantum low-density parity check codes without creating syndrome backlog?

Before

Pure BP-LSD and Beamsearch decoders without switching, yielding 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher logical error rates under the same simulated noise models.

But

Numerical simulations only; relies on cluster-based decoders to compute soft-output confidence; leakage error model evaluated via a Pauli approximation; hardware runs on classical CPU rather than fully parallelized FPGA.

Tools

sliding window decoding · cluster norm metric · bivariate bicycle (BB) codes · Stim Monte Carlo simulations · BP-LSD, UF, Tesseract, and Relay-BP decoders

Abstract

Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the textttBP-LSD decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the textttBeamsearch decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.

item.title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Noisy stabilizer QEC cycles with leakage map to classical Markov processes over joint syndrome and leakage configurations, with logical Pauli channels tied to transitions; yields an exact transfer-matrix expression for logical memory survival probability.

Grade 0.446 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Alex Kwiatkowski, Aaron J. Friedman

Asks

How to model multi-cycle logical stabilizer QEC performance under physical qubit leakage errors using twirling approximations?

Before

Stabilizer QEC cycles with purely Pauli-stochastic noise mapped to Markov processes over syndrome states without leakage.

But

Applies to stabilizer QEC cycles; relies on the leakage-dephased Pauli twirling approximation.

Tools

leakage-dephased Pauli twirling · classical Markov chains · transfer-matrix method · stabilizer formalism

Abstract

The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

item.title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Photon distinguishability threshold decreases from 0.136% to 0.080% under Shor(2,2) encoding for all-photonic resource state preparation, but remains comparable for repeat-until-success (RUS) generation at 0.256% unencoded and 0.271% encoded.

Grade 0.434 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Katia Hakem, Grégoire de Gliniasty, Nathan Shettell, Paul Hilaire, Stephen C. Wein

Figure

Six-ring resource state graph. Vertices represent qubits in |+⟩ and edges represent CZ gates; highlighted vertices show the stabilizer generator K1=Z6X1Z2.

Asks

How does partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and linear-optical fusion measurements affect the fault tolerance and logical encoding benefits of fusion-based quantum computing architectures?

But

First-order distinguishability expansion in D, dual-rail encoding with ideal photon-number-resolving detectors, specific to 6-ring fusion networks.

Tools

Orthogonal bad-bit distinguishability noise model · 6-ring fusion network · Shor(2,2) code encoding · Monte Carlo fault-tolerance simulations · Repeat-until-success emitter entangling gates

Abstract

Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.
